overview: The Medford School Committee is the governing body responsible for setting educational policies, adopting operating and capital budgets, overseeing district leadership, and approving collective bargaining agreements for the Medford Public Schools. Chaired by the Mayor and composed of elected committee members, the committee deliberates on district infrastructure, curriculum, student support services, and administrative operations. The archive's records document regular and special meetings spanning from February 2021 through October 2026 across four successive terms. Over this period, the committee navigated pandemic response, school safety reviews, major facility repairs, labor negotiations, leadership transitions, and the launch of the Medford Comprehensive High School building project with the Massachusetts School Building Authority. At its most recent meetings, the committee advanced districtwide capital projects, including geothermal and heat pump HVAC replacements at elementary schools, monitored expanded after-school programming, and continued preparations for the high school project and elementary school reassignment policies.

threads.name: Medford Comprehensive High School building project
threads.summary: In 2022, the committee initiated a Statement of Interest to the Massachusetts School Building Authority (MSBA) Core Program to address extensive infrastructure and energy efficiency deficiencies at Medford High School (M20#18, M29#3, M31#1). Following acceptance into the MSBA eligibility phase in late 2023, the committee formally established the Medford Comprehensive High School Building Committee governance structure and appointed member rosters in early 2024 (M75#5, M78#6, M80#7, M85#8). The committee selected Left Field as the Owner's Project Manager in 2025 and conducted site reviews, educational planning, and community design forums to evaluate renovation versus new construction alternatives (M117#4, M124#5, M129#6, M140#5, M150#3). After discovering a 1967 Department of Conservation and Recreation deed restriction on Edgerly Field that eliminated several design layouts, the body modified options to avoid restricted land and revised space plans for MSBA submission (M153#2, M156#3, M158#7). Work remains ongoing as the committee refines schematic designs, updates project committee membership, and evaluates municipal space alternatives and local authorization schedules (M158#8, M160#7, M161#9).

threads.name: School facilities and HVAC modernization
threads.summary: Confronting recurring heating, ventilation, and cooling failures across aging campuses, the committee directed facility assessments and enacted policies restricting future purchases of fossil-fuel building equipment (M06#9, M67#6, M87#6, M87#13). To address cooling system breakdowns and obsolete refrigerants, the committee approved a $25.7 million bond recommendation and authorized construction-management-at-risk procurement for comprehensive HVAC upgrades at McGlynn and Andrews middle schools (M108#6, M112#6, M121#7). A 2025 districtwide facilities assessment identified $83.7 million in required repairs over five years, leading to prioritized capital requests for roofs, masonry, and mechanical systems (M135#3, M138#6, M143#7). The committee subsequently submitted MSBA Accelerated Repair applications and approved schematic designs for roof replacements and heat pump installations at elementary schools (M119#1, M158#5, M161#4). Most recently, the committee selected a ground-source geothermal HVAC system for Missituk Elementary and approved a construction-management-at-risk delivery method for Roberts Elementary (M165#4, M165#5).

threads.name: Superintendent leadership and administrative transitions
threads.summary: In 2021, the committee granted a four-year contract extension to Superintendent Dr. Marice Edouard-Vincent and conducted annual performance reviews guided by district improvement goals (M04#6, M10#1, M64#2, M76#8). Following contract strategy sessions in mid-2024, Dr. Edouard-Vincent announced her departure after seven years of leadership in early 2025 (M95#2, M102#1, M112#3, M113#9). The committee appointed Assistant Superintendent Dr. Suzanne Galusi as Interim Superintendent in December 2024, subsequently approving her employment agreement and transitional leadership plan (M111#2, M113#3, M114#2). After evaluating Dr. Galusi's performance and gathering community survey data regarding leadership priorities, the committee voted to appoint her permanent superintendent in February 2026 (M140#6, M141#4). The committee finalized a three-year contract with Superintendent Galusi in May 2026 and later aligned the annual superintendent evaluation schedule with the academic year (M151#6, M158#11, M162#6).

threads.name: Collective bargaining and labor relations
threads.summary: The committee regularly negotiates collective bargaining agreements and memoranda of understanding across multiple education bargaining units (M01#1, M02#9, M33#7). Negotiations with the Medford Teachers Association involved an impasse and state mediation in 2022 before reaching a four-year agreement altering the school day, followed by another successor three-year contract ratified in 2025 (M38#5, M42#4, M48#5, M123#3). Agreements were also negotiated and ratified for administrative assistants, custodians, school administrators, and cafeteria workers (M39#1, M69#1, M81#4, M92#2, M93#2, M126#6, M144#1). To address severe staffing shortages and pay equity, the committee repeatedly approved multi-year agreements and wage adjustments for paraprofessionals and Kids' Corner personnel (M41#2, M96#2, M96#3, M130#2). The committee also approved a successor agreement with the Massachusetts Nurses Association through fiscal year 2028 as labor negotiations across bargaining units remain recurring business (M132#1, M154#2, M158#1).

threads.name: Elementary school capacity, overcrowding, and grade configuration
threads.summary: Early in the archive, the committee oversaw the renaming of Christopher Columbus Elementary School to the Missituk School following advisory committee recommendations and community testimony (M02#13, M07#11, M09#3). Shifting enrollment patterns subsequently created severe overcrowding at Roberts Elementary School, leading staff and caregivers to request formal redistricting (M18#5, M98#8, M99#6). In response, the committee approved relocating preschool classrooms from Roberts to Missituk, created a strategic space planning task force, and initiated a facilities utilization study (M122#4, M127#6, M127#7). When consultants presented grade-restructuring options, the committee gathered public survey feedback and voted to delay any proposed 5-8 middle school reconfiguration until at least the 2028-2029 school year (M136#5, M137#5, M160#4). The committee also initiated drafting a formal intra-district elementary school reassignment policy to govern alternative placement requests and establish enrollment buffers (M132#11, M164#5).

threads.name: Before and after school care programming
threads.summary: Throughout the recorded period, the committee routinely addressed capacity limits, waitlists, and staffing challenges in district-run before- and after-school programs (M03#4, M04#9, M19#9, M47#4). The committee approved program restructuring, including replacing kindergarten waitlists with lotteries, establishing sliding-scale tuition structures, and implementing annual rate and wage adjustments (M23#6, M54#5, M56#8, M81#7, M122#1). In 2024, the district established a pilot partnership with City Year to place AmeriCorps members in schools to support classroom instruction and increase after-school capacity (M93#4, M100#3, M100#5). The committee then engaged the Belmont After School Enrichment Collaborative (BASIC) for a consultancy and approved recommendations adding 150 seats, full-time site coordinators, and new early-pickup tuition rates (M125#2, M128#5, M130#3, M151#4, M151#5). By late 2026, administrative reports confirmed program enrollment had expanded by 50 percent alongside significant reductions in waitlist numbers (M162#5, M165#3).

threads.name: School safety, culture, and student disciplinary policy
threads.summary: Incidents of high school violence and a December 2022 stabbing prompted extensive public concern, leading the committee to adopt safety action plans, bathroom monitoring protocols, anonymous reporting systems, and a culture assessment by consultant Michael Welch (M17#4, M17#12, M48#4, M49#5, M49#6, M58#7). The committee focused on narrowing exclusionary discipline, piloting restorative justice programs, requiring disaggregated suspension reports, and creating standardized student incident reporting forms (M22#5, M44#8, M46#11, M49#8, M82#12, M87#7, M128#13). District policies were repeatedly updated to align with statutory standards and student equity goals, including revisions to the bullying prevention plan, gender identity non-discrimination policies, and federal Title IX grievance procedures (M57#8, M65#6, M73#6, M78#7, M105#1, M107#6, M152#6). Student voice was integrated through formal Student Advisory Council presentations concerning homework time limits, backpack policies, and transportation safety (M72#2, M72#3, M83#2, M90#1, M133#7, M145#7). Facilities-focused safety initiatives also included safety inspections, bathroom security funding, and the construction of an accessible playground at McGlynn Elementary (M13#7, M47#5, M76#10, M91#6, M103#2, M110#9).

threads.name: Annual operating budgets and fiscal planning
threads.summary: The committee managed annual operating budgets amid projected municipal deficits, expiring federal pandemic relief (ESSER) funds, and rising special education and transportation costs (M01#10, M07#10, M10#2, M36#5, M37#6, M64#4). In early 2024, the administration disclosed a projected $2.5 million mid-year FY24 budget deficit, which was remediated through spending freezes, grant reallocations, and accounting corrections (M79#4, M82#5). Responding to proposed administrative and staff cuts, the committee submitted a level-service FY25 budget request of $79.4 million, approved a final $77.75 million budget, and adopted formal policies establishing budget preparation schedules and capital planning phases (M89#9, M91#9, M93#7, M93#9). Following the approval of municipal ballot questions 7 and 8 in late 2024, the committee allocated override funds through a supplemental budget appropriation toward restored positions, facilities, and collective bargaining reserves (M100#8, M108#7, M113#7). Subsequent budget development included joint fiscal sessions with the City Council and budget approvals closing operating gaps through fund balance adjustments and municipal stabilization funding (M145#5, M146#3, M158#4, M165#6).
